# Empirical application

Hedonic price regressions read the value of a local amenity off the
cross-section of property values \citep[see][]{rosen1974,bishop2020}, and
regulatory designations are a standard source of exogenous variation in them
\citep[see][]{greenstonegallagher2008}. Air quality is the amenity with the
longest such literature. The regressor of interest is almost always entered
linearly, and we relax that here, on a two-period county panel whose instrument
is discrete because the regulation that generates it is a rule on thresholds.
The section illustrates the estimator of Section 3 on that panel and claims
nothing beyond the illustration; what it does not establish is set out in the
last subsection rather than left to be discovered there.

The data are the county panel \citet{chay2005} assembled to measure
how the 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments capitalised into property values. The file
holds 989 counties. One candidate control, per-capita expenditure on pollution
abatement, is missing in all 989 rows and is dropped as an empty column rather
than as item non-response, which leaves 22 usable controls and not 23; six
counties are missing the local-fiscal block, which leaves an analysis sample of
$n=983$ (Table S34 of the supplement). Descriptive statistics are in Table S16.

Write $Y_{ij}$ for the log of county $i$'s median property value in
$j\in\{1970,1980\}$, $X_{ij}$ for its mean concentration of total suspended
particulates in $\mu$g/m$^3$, $W_i$ for its 1975 nonattainment designation, and
$\Delta Z_i$ for an intercept together with $d_Z$ differenced county
characteristics, at $d_Z=5$ throughout except where a table reports a second
size. That is the
differenced model of Section 2 term by term: a continuous endogenous scalar
entering through $\vdagger$, a discrete instrument, a differenced control
vector, and a county effect the differencing removes. Just under a third of the
analysis sample is designated, at a mean of $0.303$ (Table S35 of the
supplement).

The intercept is not decoration and A4(ii) requires it. Read against A1b(iv),
that clause forces $\Delta Z$ to carry exactly one constant coordinate, which in
a differenced equation is the period effect; every specification below has
$p=d_Z+1$ with the constant in the first column, so the requirement of Section 3
holds throughout.

The object of economic interest here is $\vdagger$ and not $\theta_\dagger$.
The structural function is the hedonic price of air quality, which is what this
literature is written about; $\theta_\dagger$ collects coefficients on
demographic and fiscal controls, which are not what anyone reads the exercise
for. That inverts \cref{thm:rootn}, whose $\sqrt n$ statement is about
$\theta_\dagger$. The two roles are interchangeable across applications, and
which of them a paper is written about is a property of the question rather than
of the model; this one happens to run the opposite way to our theorem's
headline.

## The instrument

The designation rule fires on either of two triggers. A county is designated if
its annual geometric mean exceeds the standard, or if its second-highest daily
reading does, and $298$ of the $983$ counties are designated on one or the
other. We read $W$ as the pair of triggers rather than as their disjunction,
which gives a four-valued instrument: $685$ counties trigger neither, $114$ the
bad-day rule alone, $66$ the annual mean alone, and $118$ both, the last three
being the cell sizes \cref{tab:app-localise} prints. The four cells
are ordered in baseline particulates, at $58.0$, $73.3$, $79.9$ and
$97.8\,\mu$g/m$^3$. They are not ordered in the decadal change, at $-7.1$,
$-13.7$, $-9.9$ and $-21.0$: every cell falls, the base cell least and the
both-triggers cell most, but the two single-trigger cells reverse between them.
Those two rows of cell means are computed on the analysis sample and are
tabulated nowhere; the notes to \cref{tab:app-localise} say where they and the
base-cell size are produced.
The refinement discards nothing: a county is designated in the binary
reading if and only if it lies outside the first cell, at all $983$
observations.

The reason for reading the designation at $\mathsf L=4$ is methodological and
not empirical. Four cells are what the rule says, so the binary indicator is a
coarsening of the datum rather than the datum itself, and a coarsening imposes
fewer restrictions than the rule supplies. Under A1 the three contrasts the four
cells generate are further restrictions on the same $\vdagger$, by
\cref{prp:localise}, so a reader who takes the binary reading is discarding
restrictions the same assumption already licenses. That is what the
general-$\mathsf L$ theory of Sections 2 to 4 is for, and this is where it is
exercised. What the extra cells do not buy should be said in the same breath,
because each of the three is easy to assume: they do not buy identification,
since a coarsening imposes fewer restrictions and a finer instrument therefore
makes A1b(iii) weaker rather than stronger; they do not buy testability, which
is present already at $\mathsf L=2$, where the restriction is a continuum of
equations against one unknown function; and they do not buy instrument strength,
since splitting an instrument creates no variation.

What they do buy is a decomposition, and it is the one \cref{prp:localise}
describes. At $\mathsf L=4$ the restriction A1 carries is three cell systems
rather than one, so the moment splits into three pieces indexed by the contrasts
$\widetilde W_l$, and a piece far from zero at the common fit is a cell in which
the four-valued reading conflicts with $\hat\varphi$. All three exceed their own
reference: the bad-day cell at $p=0.039$, the annual-mean cell at $0.006$ and the
joint cell at $0.003$, on $78$, $12$ and $6$ null draws at or above the observed
norm out of $B=2{,}000$ (\cref{tab:app-localise}). The
reading runs one way only. A small $p$ localises a conflict to that cell; a large
one exonerates nothing, since consistency across cells is necessary and not
sufficient for A1 by \cref{prp:localise}(iii), and the false-negative rate of the
attribution is not priced anywhere in this paper. We report the three cells and
draw no ordering from them.

The instrument moves the regressor. Nonattainment lowers the decadal change in
mean particulates by $8.37$ to $9.11\,\mu$g/m$^3$ across the four control sets,
which is between $12.7$ and $13.8$ per cent of the 1970 mean of
$66.0\,\mu$g/m$^3$, and it does so at the $1$ per cent level at every one of them
(\cref{tab:app-firststage}, Panel A), on the state-clustered standard error that
table's stars are computed from and on the robust one alike. On the robust
standard errors the first stage is strong, at $F$ between $21.3$ and $24.5$. We
report the clustered figure instead, because designation was made at the level
of the Air Quality Control Region and A0 assumes independent sampling; state is
the coarsest proxy the file supports. Clustered, $F$ runs from $10.6$ with no
controls to $13.1$ at the widest set, so the first stage clears the conventional
weak-instrument threshold of ten at every control set, and clears it with little
room at the narrowest. That table runs
on the binary coarsening, which by the paragraph above agrees with
$\{W>0\}$ at every county, and its four columns vary the control set rather than
the instrument.

The linear benchmark is the object the nonparametric estimate has to beat, and
it lands beside the number the literature reports. The reduced form is $0.0462$ at the
headline control set, and linear instrumental variables give
$-5.519\times10^{-3}$ log points per $\mu$g/m$^3$ (\cref{tab:app-firststage},
Panels B and C); at the 1970 mean that is an elasticity of $-0.364$, against the
$-0.20$ to $-0.35$ \citet{chay2005} report from linear instrumental variables on
this design. It sits just past the more negative end of that range, by $0.014$,
and reproduces its sign and its order of magnitude rather than falling inside it.
The reduced form more than halves as
controls are added, from $0.0462$ at five controls to $0.0209$ at twenty-two.

A4(i) survives the refinement, and the two quantities the assumption prices are
worth reporting because they behave differently. The multinomial propensity,
fitted on the headline control set and projected onto the truncation set of
\cref{def:hatT} at $\varepsilon_\varrho=0.01$, has in-sample minimum
$\min_l\hat\varrho_l=0.0115$, which clears the floor $\varepsilon_\varrho=0.01$
the truncation is run at, so the truncation binds on none of the $983$ rows of an
in-sample fit. That floor is an admissible one because A4(i) asks only for
$\varepsilon_\varrho\in(0,1/\mathsf L)$, which is $(0,0.25)$ at $\mathsf L=4$;
the $0.25$ bounds how large a floor may be set and is not a level $\hat\varrho$
is asked to reach.
It does bind on the fit the estimator actually uses. \Cref{def:crossfit}(a)
fits $\hat\varrho$ on the complement of each fold and evaluates it on the fold,
and over the $29{,}500$ cross-fitted evaluations one estimation run makes, the
projection binds on $0.997$ per cent of them, at a pre-projection minimum of
$4.3\times10^{-5}$; at the binary coarsening it binds on none
(\cref{tab:app-theta}). It binds harder once the sample is reweighted. Under the
$\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ multiplier weights of Section 6.3 the binding share has
median $0.41$ per cent and reaches $4.37$ per cent, at a smallest pre-projection
$\hat\varrho_l$ of $2.5\times10^{-4}$, and $81$ of the $99$ replications bind
somewhere. Those four numbers are per-replication diagnostics of the multiplier
arm and are printed in no table; they come from
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_06\_phi\_mult.R}, run object
\texttt{quality\_reports/application/app\_tsp\_phi\_mult.rds}, which is the arm
Table S42 of the supplement summarises at the percentiles rather than at the
truncation. Where the projection binds, A1 holds at $\hat\varrho$ and fails at the
truncated propensity the estimator substitutes for it, so those evaluations are
not covered by the assumption; the theory prices this as a bias term rather than
excluding it, and the shares above are how large the affected set is here. The
implied covariance clears the bound of \eqref{eq:omegafloor} with room, at
$\lambda_{\min}(\hat\Omega)=0.0113$ against $\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf
L=0.0025$. No cells need merging, which matters because merging strengthens
A1b(iii) and gives back the restrictions the refinement was taken for.

The designation in hand is not the designation that was made. Between 1972 and
1978 nonattainment status under the Clean Air Act was assigned at the level of
the Air Quality Control Region, and the county-level variable in this file is an
imputation from monitor readings. \citet{cropper2023} quantify the discrepancy:
the two definitions disagree about which counties are treated on a scale that is
not a rounding error, and the estimated reduction in total suspended
particulates attenuates from $10.2$ and $9.1\,\mu$g/m$^{3}$ across their two
panels under the official designation to $6.0$ and $7.7$ under the county-level
definition this section adopts, keeping its sign and its order of magnitude. The
condition under which the imputed variable is admissible here is non-differential
misclassification: the imputation may mislabel a county, but the probability that
it does so must not depend on $\Delta U$ given $\Delta Z$. Under that condition
$W$ remains a valid instrument and is merely less relevant, and A1 survives;
under the alternative the estimator is inconsistent rather than imprecise, so no
sample size repairs it. We assume the condition and do not test it.

## The estimator on this panel

One property of the estimator changed between the diagnostics above and the
estimates below, and it is a hypothesis the theory consumes rather than a tuning
choice. The $x$-direction kernel is the supplement's boundary family at
$p_K=8$, so every truncated moment \eqref{eq:truncmom} asks for vanishes: across
$j=0,\dots,7$, and over the $1{,}966$ design points of this panel, the worst
departure is $2.6\times10^{-10}$, the boundary layer and the two endpoints
included. The engine it replaces renormalised to unit mass at each design point,
which realises the $j=0$ member alone and leaves the orders $3\le j\le 7$ as
large as $38.2985$ in the layer. Two clauses of the theory turn on the
difference. The first is the observable of the supplement's proposition on
$\hat{\mathcal A}_\varphi$, namely $\int_{\mathcal X}\hat\nu\,dx=0$, which is
exactly zero by construction where the unadjusted engine put it at
$-4.58\times10^{-5}$, or $41.2$ per cent of $\sup_x|\hat\nu|$; that clause is
what puts the adjoint's range inside $\mathcal V$, so the unadjusted engine did
not satisfy a condition \cref{thm:rootn} consumes and both adjusted ones do. The
second is the boundary bias, which the enforced moments put at $O(h_x^{p_K})$
where the renormalisation left it at $O(h_x)$ within a bandwidth of an endpoint.
Every number in this subsection and the next moved as a result: at $d_Z=5$ and
$\mathsf L=4$, on identical streams, no coordinate of $\hat\theta$ moves from the
renormalised arm by more than $0.0470$, which is $0.218$ clustered standard
errors, and $\hat\varphi$ moves by at most $0.0081$ in the sup norm.

The family is not free, and the same ablation prices it. Vanishing moments to
order $p_K=8$ force a sign-indefinite kernel, and three readings record what the
shipped family costs against the renormalised engine it replaced: the running
integral $S(v;X)$ that the adjoint carries ranges over $[-0.388,1.388]$ where
the renormalised engine held it in $[0,1]$; it is non-monotone at all $1{,}966$
design points of this panel, where the renormalised engine was monotone at every
one; and $\sup_\varsigma|\Theta_I|$ is $17.43$ against the $0.873$ of the
interior member. On these three readings the shipped family is the worse of the
two, and we report that beside the benefit because the same script computes
both. No kernel with vanishing moments beyond the second can be non-negative, so
the sign is the price \eqref{eq:truncmom} charges rather than a defect of this
implementation. What it threatens is the conditioning of the Gram the family
induces, which stays invertible on the realised $I$ at
$\lambda_{\min}(\mathsf G(I))=1.51\times10^{-5}$.

\Cref{tab:app-theta} reports $\hat\theta$ at the headline control set, at
$\mathsf L=4$ and at the binary coarsening, on the same cross-fitting partition
stream, at a common $\varepsilon_\varrho=0.01$ and at a common iteration cap
$\bar m=60$, which is a calibration constant of this section and not the
$\bar m_n$ of \eqref{eq:cap}, so the two columns vary one factor. There is no
$\Delta$TSP coordinate in $\hat\theta$, and the point is worth making because
the coefficient a hedonic reader looks for is not in that table: the endogenous
regressor enters through $\vdagger$ alone, as $\vdagger(X_{i2})-\vdagger(X_{i1})$,
and $\theta_\dagger$ collects the coefficients on the differenced controls.

The two columns agree on sign and on order of magnitude at every coordinate, and
we put the agreement no more strongly than that. Per capita income is $0.7112$
with a clustered standard error of $0.2027$ at $\mathsf L=4$, against $0.6057$
$(0.1862)$ at the binary coarsening; population is $0.3102$ $(0.0754)$ against
$0.3433$ $(0.0838)$. Measured in units of the four-cell column's own clustered
standard error, the gaps are $0.23$ at the constant, $0.52$ at income, $0.44$ at
population, $0.21$ at the unemployment rate, $0.12$ at manufacturing employment
and $0.08$ at the high-school share, so no coordinate moves by as much as
$0.53$ of a standard error and four of the six move by less than a quarter of
one. That is the
expected direction of no effect rather than a null result: under A1 the surplus
contrasts are further restrictions on the same $\vdagger$, so they buy
localisation and not a different answer, and a large shift between
the columns would have been evidence against A1 or against the binary estimate.
The clustered standard error is smaller in the four-cell column at five of the
six coordinates and larger at per capita income, at $0.2027$ against $0.1862$, so
the extra cells do not buy precision coordinate by coordinate on this panel.

What the design does now separate is the cardinality from the iteration cap,
which earlier drafts could not. \Cref{tab:app-theta-cap} adds a third arm, the
binary coarsening at the cap $\bar m=15$ that its own cardinality would have set,
and the cap alone moves that column by $\max_j|\Delta\hat\theta_j|=0.1930$,
concentrated at the high-school share, with manufacturing employment next at
$0.1334$ and per capita income third at $0.0447$, all differences taken on the
unrounded estimates rather than on the four digits the table prints. The cap is
therefore not a
second-order detail of this comparison, and it moves the binary column further
than the cardinality does, whose own largest coordinate move is $0.1243$.

The standard errors in both tables are conditional on a hypothesis the estimator
does not impose, and we report the size of the gap rather than assume it away.
\Cref{cor:centarity} makes N1 a condition on a $p\times(\mathsf L-1)$ matrix,
hence $p(\mathsf L-1)$ scalar conditions rather than $p$, and (T-2) assumes it at
$L_\star$. The anchor this estimator removes is a constant per $(j,l)$ and not a
function of $\Delta Z$, so it satisfies no version of N1 beyond the unconditional
one; because projecting on a basis containing an intercept preserves sample
means, what \cref{tab:app-n1} reports is the smallest N1 defect any constant
anchor can reach. At $\mathsf L=4$ that defect is $0.2522$ after debiasing, with a
$95$ per cent upper bound of $0.4021$, which is $0.137$ of $\|\hat L\|$, and a
permutation $p$ of $0.206$ on the largest of the eighteen entries; the two binary
arms are smaller on that statistic, at $0.0245$ and $0.0156$ debiased, and are also
insignificant, at $p=0.394$ and $p=0.455$. Those two arms are the paired column
of \cref{tab:app-theta} and the binary ladder of Table S38 of the supplement,
which differ from each other in the cross-fitting stream, the truncation level
and the iteration cap, so the gap between $0.0245$ and $0.0156$ carries three
factors and is not a replication of one number. Two readings are declined. This is not evidence of absence: at
$n=983$ the defect is not resolvable from zero, so the non-rejection is a
statement about the power of the check and not about N1. And no moment-level
diagnostic could have substituted for it, because
$E[\widetilde W_l\hat L_{jl}\mid\Delta Z]=0$ holds automatically under A1
whatever the anchor is, so a moment that looks orthogonal is consistent with N1
failing at every entry. Inference in this section is conditional on N1, and by
\cref{prp:orthog}(iii) what its failure would cost is the propensity direction of
the orthogonality, at the full rate $r_n$ and undamped.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\Cref{fig:app-phi} draws $\hat\varphi$ at the headline control set, normalised
at the pooled median of $X$, and \cref{tab:app-phi} prints it at eleven
percentiles of the pooled distribution. The curve drawn is the four-cell fit,
which is the arm the bootstrap of the next subsection is run on. The
binary-coarsening curve does not sit on top of it. At the common cap the sup gap
between the two is $0.0327$, which is $85$ per cent of the four-cell curve's own
range of $0.0383$, while the root-mean-square gap over the grid is $0.0136$
against that same range, so the two curves separate at some points of the support
and not on average. The binary curve's own range is $0.0634$ against the
four-cell curve's $0.0383$, a factor of $1.65$. Those three readings are internal
to the two arms being compared. We also quote the gap in sampling units, and
there the scale is borrowed: at its worst grid point the gap is $6.09$ pointwise
bootstrap standard deviations, and the root-mean-square gap is $0.96$ times the
median pointwise standard deviation. Both denominators are the bootstrap standard
deviation of the band arm that \cref{fig:app-phi} draws, which is the only arm
here on which a bootstrap is run; the three arms of \cref{tab:app-theta-cap} are
point estimates and carry none. Numerator and denominator are therefore computed
on different estimators of the same $\vdagger$, the first cross-fitted over folds
and partitions and the second a full-sample pass at a fixed $\hat\theta$, which
makes those two ratios an order-of-magnitude sampling scale and not a test. The
sentence about where the curves separate is taken on the absolute gaps and on the
four-cell range, and not on them.

The comparison we do not report is worth naming, because it is the one an earlier
draft made and it reads the other way. Letting the cap move with the cardinality,
as its calibration would, puts the sup gap at $0.0081$ and the root-mean-square
gap at $0.41$ of the same borrowed standard deviation, which would license the
sentence that the two cardinalities agree. It is an artefact of two effects that nearly cancel. The cap
alone moves the binary curve by $0.0380$ in the sup norm, larger than the
$0.0327$ cardinality gap it is being netted against, and
\cref{tab:app-theta-cap} shows
the same cancellation in $\hat\theta$. *Every numerator quoted above is taken on
the three arms of \cref{tab:app-theta-cap}*, which share one cross-fitting
stream; the three denominators that are standard deviations are taken on the band
arm instead, for the reason given above, and they are the only borrowed quantity
in these two paragraphs. \emph{The band arm's own readings follow, none of them a
standard deviation, and where one is set against a three-arm figure the sentence
says which}: that arm is a different estimator of the same
$\vdagger$, its four-cell curve has range $0.0349$ against the $0.0383$ here and
differs from it by $0.0066$ in the sup norm, and it puts the two-factor sup gap
at $0.0143$. We therefore report the one-factor
comparison throughout and read the two-factor number as measuring nothing.

The curve is not monotone, and the sign the hedonic reading asks for is
delivered on part of the support and not on the rest. It runs from $+0.0175$ log
points at the 5th percentile of $X$, or $31.4\,\mu$g/m$^3$, to $+0.0090$ at the
95th, or $100.2\,\mu$g/m$^3$, and it rises at $32$ of its $59$ grid steps and
falls at $27$. Those steps fall into four monotone stretches. It descends to
$-0.0174$ at $48.7\,\mu$g/m$^3$, the 28th percentile; climbs to $+0.0150$ at
$68.5$, the 71st; falls to $+0.0001$ at $86.4$, the 89th; and rises again over
the last four steps. Its whole range is $0.0349$, and its largest sustained
movement, at $+1.64\times10^{-3}$ log points per $\mu$g/m$^3$ between the trough
and the peak, runs the wrong way for the hedonic reading.

The linear instrumental-variables slope on the same sample and the same controls
is $-5.519\times10^{-3}$ log points per $\mu$g/m$^3$, which over the
$68.8\,\mu$g/m$^3$ separating the 5th and the 95th percentiles is $0.380$ log
points. The nonparametric estimate's whole range is $0.0349$, which bounds its
movement between any two points of the support and is under a tenth of that;
between those same two percentiles it moves $-0.0085$, which is $2.2$ per cent
of what the linear slope delivers over the same interval and smaller than the
pointwise bootstrap standard deviation at either endpoint. It is nowhere as
steep either: its steepest single
descending step is $-3.28\times10^{-3}$, or $59.5$ per cent of the linear slope,
that share taken on the unrounded step and slope and not on the three digits
printed, which give $59.4$, and no descending step reaches it. *The two estimates therefore
disagree about the level of the gradient and not only about its shape.* Every
sentence of this reading is a statement about the point estimate. The constant
slope the linear specification imposes is not a feature of $\hat\varphi$ at any
point of the support, and the sign it imposes fails on the two rising stretches,
which between them carry $48.8$ per cent of the pooled distribution of $X$; we
put it no higher than that, and in particular we do not call it a negative
result. The envelope drawn in Section 6.3 has a median width over the
evaluation grid of $1.33$ times the curve's whole range, and that section
declines to infer from the envelope in either direction, so nothing here rules a
constant slope out. What
the estimator delivers is a point estimate that does not reproduce one.

## The bootstrap

Valid uniform inference on $\hat\varphi$ does not exist in this model, and the
obstruction is a property of the estimator rather than of this application.
Uniform confidence bands for ill-posed problems are built on a source condition
written in the spectral calculus of $T^\ast T$ and on completeness of the
instrument, and neither is available here: the operator equation of Section 2 is
nonlinear in $\varphi$, so there is no adjoint in which to write the condition,
and a $W$ with four values delivers completeness no more than a two-valued one
does \citep[see][]{severini2006,babiiflorens2025}. Pointwise inference does exist
for nonlinearly ill-posed conditional moment models, and \citet{chen2012b} give
sieve Wald and quasi-likelihood-ratio confidence sets for the evaluation
functional, valid whether or not that functional is $\sqrt n$-estimable. Their
theory is indexed by a sieve dimension, whereas the regularisation index of
\cref{def:lfstep} is a Landweber iteration count, and we are not aware of any
procedure that transfers between the two. The runs reported below fix that index
at the cap, so it is not random here; that removes one obstruction and leaves the
two above, which are the binding ones.

We therefore follow the convention of the companion paper
\citep{centorrinofeveflorens2019}, which estimates the same operator equation from
a discrete instrument under the same regularisation: a point estimate, a
bootstrap band drawn to show variability, and one sentence saying what the band
is not. *The envelope below illustrates the variability of $\hat\varphi$ and is
not a confidence set. No coverage is claimed for it and none is computed.*

The band is wide against the curve it surrounds. At the 5th percentile of $X$
the fifth-to-ninety-fifth bootstrap envelope runs from $-0.0175$ to $+0.0436$, a
width of $0.0611$; at the 95th percentile it runs from $-0.0261$ to $+0.0506$, a
width of $0.0767$. The curve's entire range is $0.0349$, and over the whole
sixty-point evaluation grid the median width of the envelope is $0.0463$, so the
typical envelope is $1.33$ times everything the curve does. It pinches
to $0.0042$ near the anchor, where the normalisation puts it, and widens towards
both tails, at $23$ of the $29$ steps to its left and at $28$ of the $30$ steps
to its right. The envelope excludes zero at one of the eleven levels
\cref{tab:app-phi} prints, the 30th percentile, where it runs from $-0.0426$ to
$-0.0004$, and at $6$ of the $60$ grid points, five of them consecutive between
$49.5$ and $51.9\,\mu$g/m$^3$, where the envelope is entirely negative, and one
isolated at $67.4$, where it is entirely positive. We give those widths
and those counts as a description of the envelope and we draw no inference from
them in either direction: no coverage is claimed for the envelope, so the six
exclusions are not evidence that the sign of the hedonic gradient is pinned down
there, and the fifty-four non-exclusions are not evidence that it is
unidentified.

The bootstrap's own convergence record is in Panel B, and it does not explain
the width. All $99$ replications returned a finite curve, with no errors and no
non-finite values. The realised stopping index $\hat m_\varphi$, which is the
$\hat m^{(k)}$ of \cref{def:lfstep}(c) written with the letter this section uses
for it, equals $60$ in every one of them, at a minimum and a maximum of $60$. *That number is the
iteration budget and not a selected quantity, and nothing should be read from
it.* Section 3's discrepancy rule is run at $\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$ here, which
disables the branch that could stop early, and the patience is set equal to the
cap, so budget exhaustion is the only terminus a solve has. The distribution of
$\hat m_\varphi$ is therefore degenerate by construction rather than by
convergence, and in particular the absence of replications at
$\hat m_\varphi=1$ is not evidence that none was at risk of returning its
initial condition: under this configuration none could. The regularisation the
band prices is the one the cap supplies.

What the record does show is that the width is not the footprint of shrinkage.
The bootstrap median curve, drawn dashed in
\cref{fig:app-phi}, spans $0.0377$ against the point estimate's $0.0349$, or
$108.1$ per cent of it, the ratio taken on the unrounded spans and not on the
four digits printed, and departs from the point estimate by at most $0.0049$ at
any grid point. A resampling scheme that shrank the curve would return a median
below the point estimate's range and not above it. The level of the curve
remains unidentified separately from its shape, and the anchor's own standard
deviation across resamples is $0.63\,\mu$g/m$^3$, which is a dispersion in the
particulate level the curves are re-centred at and not in log points.

Two mechanisms could produce a width like that, and we ran three further schemes
to try to separate them, because one would make the width an artefact of the
resampling scheme and the other would make it a property of the estimator. A
resample of $n$ counties with
replacement leaves roughly $37$ per cent of the draw as duplicates, which give
the integration operator repeated rows, and it halves the information, since
weights that are multinomial have Kish effective sample size $n/2$, here $492$.
Weights drawn i.i.d. $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ have the same first two moments and the
same effective sample size but duplicate nothing; subsamples of $621$ and of
$492$ distinct counties, drawn without replacement, vary the information while
holding duplication at zero. The schemes are set out in Table S41 of the
supplement, beside the full-sample fit.

*The comparison is not evaluable, and we report it as such.* The three criteria
that would have separated the two mechanisms are all statements about
$\hat m_\varphi$, and $\hat m_\varphi$ is $60$ in every replication of every
scheme and in the full-sample fit, for the reason given above: at
$\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$ the discrepancy
branch is dead and patience equals the cap, so a solve that returns at all
returns the cap. All three criteria are therefore satisfied by construction and
discriminate nothing, and the script records no verdict rather than a verdict
read off an unfailable test. We state what each scheme produced and claim no
preference between them.

The two bootstrap schemes produce bands of similar size and do not order
cleanly. Over the sixty-point grid the multiplier band's median width is
$0.0425$ against the resample's $0.0463$, or $8.1$ per cent narrower, the ratio
taken on the unrounded widths and not on the four digits printed, which give
$8.2$; on the
first $25$ replications of each it is $0.0356$ against $0.0412$. That summary
does not carry to the level at which it is read: the multiplier band is the
wider of the two at seven of the eleven levels \cref{tab:app-phi} prints and the
narrower at four. It is wider at the 5th percentile, at $0.0657$ against
$0.0611$, at the 80th, at $0.0577$ against $0.0518$, at the 90th, at $0.0722$
against $0.0625$, at the 95th, at $0.0821$
against $0.0767$, and at the 70th, at $0.0444$ against $0.0421$; the two
remaining wider levels are the 40th and the anchor, at $0.0252$ against $0.0251$
and $0.0055$ against $0.0049$, differences that order nothing. It is narrower
between the 10th and the 30th and again at
the 60th, which is the four. The two
panels compared are Panel A of Table S42 of the supplement and Panel A of
\cref{tab:app-phi}. Each excludes
zero at one of those eleven levels. Each scheme's median curve overruns the
point estimate's range by about a tenth, at $111.0$ per cent under the
multiplier weights and $108.1$ under the resample, which is the statistic of the
preceding paragraph read at both schemes and is a property of those curves and
not of the envelopes around them. None of this makes either band valid: no coverage is claimed for
either, and the obstruction is the one stated at the head of this subsection.

## What the illustration shows

The estimator runs on this panel and returns the two objects it is built to
return: a slope vector with a clustered standard error, at either cardinality of
the instrument, and a structural curve whose shape contradicts the constant
slope the linear specification imposes. That is the whole of what the section
claims.

At $n=983$ it claims nothing about the asymptotics, and there are now two
reasons for that rather than one. Evaluated at
$(\mu,r)=(2,\tfrac83)$, the frontier-clearing configuration the Monte Carlo
names, the
frontier \eqref{eq:frontier} is met at no control set that also satisfies
A4(ii): it fails outright once any control is entered, and the one rung at which
it holds is the intercept-only rung, which A4(ii) excludes because at
$\alpha=\tfrac12$ the sieve-entropy condition admits no integer sieve dimension
and \cref{thm:rootn} is vacuous there (Table S46 of the supplement). The second reason is the cardinality arm
of the Monte Carlo, which finds the limit law's own remainder failing to vanish
at $\mathsf L=4$ on the paper's named design (Table S22 of the supplement), in a propensity direction whose price
this panel cannot bound because the N1 defect above is not resolvable from zero
at $n=983$. The object that describes this estimator
at this sample size is therefore \cref{cor:ratefloor} and not \cref{thm:rootn}.
*The application illustrates the procedure on a design the method was built for;
it does not demonstrate that the asymptotics bind at this sample size*, and we
would rather say so than let the section be read as though they did.
